identity.title: Serial Dilution and Concentration Calculations
identity.shortDescription: Prepare a series of dilutions from one stock solution, observe how colour intensity tracks concentration, and master the c1 x V1 = c2 x V2 relationship.
identity.fullDescription: Dilution is the most-used calculation in a chemistry laboratory and the easiest to get subtly wrong. This activity uses a visibly coloured dilute copper(II) sulfate stock solution: learners measure, dilute, mix and observe the stepwise loss of colour intensity while calculating each new concentration. The reasoning transfers directly to every later quantitative activity, from titration to kinetics.

prerequisites: Understanding of molar concentration (see the 'Preparing a Standard Solution' activity).
Confident use of measuring cylinders or pipettes.

learningObjectives: Apply the dilution relationship c1 x V1 = c2 x V2 to plan a dilution series.
Carry out measured dilutions and relate the visible colour intensity to concentration.
Track units and significant figures through multi-step calculations.
expectedCompetencies: Planning a serial dilution so each step is measurable.
Distinguishing 'volume of water added' from 'total final volume'.
learningOutcomes: Calculate the concentration of each member of a dilution series from one stock value.
Demonstrate a serial dilution and explain why each step multiplies the concentration by the same factor.
Predict how the appearance of a solution changes with concentration and justify the prediction with the dilution equation.

theory.overview: Diluting a solution changes its concentration but not the amount of solute it contains. That single conservation statement generates the whole calculation: whatever volume V1 of concentration c1 is taken from the stock, the same amount of solute ends up dispersed in the new total volume V2 at concentration c2, so c1 x V1 = c2 x V2. In a serial dilution the product of each step's dilution factor gives the overall factor, which is why serial dilution can reach very small concentrations with a single measuring device.

sections.heading: Conservation of solute on dilution
sections.body: When a volume V1 of stock solution is made up to a larger total volume V2, no solute is added or removed: the amount of substance n = c1 x V1 is unchanged. Therefore c2 = c1 x V1 / V2. The units carry through directly: if c is in mol/L and V in mL on both sides the millilitres cancel and c2 comes out in mol/L.

sections.heading: Serial dilution
sections.body: In a serial dilution each diluted solution becomes the stock for the next step. If every step uses the same factor f = V1 / V2 (for example 1:10), then after k steps the concentration is c0 x f^k. Errors do not accumulate randomly in a serial dilution: a systematic error in the first step propagates to all later steps, which is why the first measurement deserves the most care.

sections.heading: Colour and concentration
sections.body: For a coloured solute at low concentration, the intensity of the observed colour increases with the amount of coloured species in the light path; halving the concentration visibly lightens the solution. Colour comparison is a qualitative observation, not a quantitative measurement: it supports the calculation, it does not replace it. (A rigorous treatment belongs to spectrophotometry and Beer-Lambert law, outside this activity's scope.)

theory.scientificBackground: The dilution equation assumes volumes are additive enough for the stated precision and that temperature is roughly constant. For dilute aqueous solutions these assumptions are adequate at school-level precision; concentrated solutions can show measurable volume changes on mixing, which is one reason dilute stocks are used here.

equations.description: Conservation of solute on dilution: the amount of solute before dilution equals the amount after.
applicableConditions: V2 is the total final volume, not the volume of water added.
assumptions: Volumes are effectively additive at the working precision.
No solute is lost during transfer.

definitions.definition: The ratio V1 / V2 by which one dilution step multiplies the concentration; overall factor of a serial dilution is the product of the step factors.
The more concentrated solution from which dilutions are prepared.

chemicals.name: Copper(II) sulfate solution (stock)
chemicals.formulaOrDescription: CuSO4(aq), approximately 0.10 mol/L, prepared by the supervising educator
chemicals.notes: Blue solution used as a visible tracer. Harmful if swallowed; very toxic to aquatic life; collect waste for metal-salt disposal.

safety.riskRationale: Dilute copper(II) sulfate is a common school reagent used at 0.1 mol/L or below, without heating or reaction steps. Copper salts are harmful if swallowed and environmentally hazardous, so ingestion and drain disposal are the controlled risks.

hazards.statement: Copper(II) sulfate is harmful if swallowed; never mouth-pipette and wash hands after handling.

evidence.notes: GHS acute toxicity classification (oral) for copper(II) sulfate per the PubChem compound entry.

hazards.statement: Copper(II) sulfate is very toxic to aquatic life; do not pour copper solutions down the drain.

evidence.notes: GHS environmental hazard classification per the PubChem compound entry.

hazards.statement: Copper(II) sulfate solution is irritating to eyes and skin; wear safety spectacles and avoid contact.

evidence.notes: GHS skin/eye irritation classification per the PubChem compound entry.

disposal: Collect all copper(II) sulfate solutions in a labelled waste container for metal-salt disposal provided by the supervising institution.
Do not dispose of copper solutions in the drain or in the environment.
Rinse measuring equipment into the waste container, not the sink.
restrictedOperations: No mouth pipetting under any circumstances.
No heating of copper solutions in this activity.
emergencyGuidance: Eye contact: rinse with plenty of water and inform the supervising educator.
Ingestion: do not induce vomiting; inform the supervising educator and seek medical advice.

procedure.overview: Prepare a 1:10 dilution series from the stock solution, calculating each concentration before you measure it. Keep the first measurement the most careful one; every later value inherits its error.

steps.title: Plan and calculate the series
steps.instructions: Label five vessels 1 to 5. Decide on a 1:10 step factor. Calculate the expected concentration of each vessel if vessel 1 is 10.0 mL of stock diluted to 100.0 mL, vessel 2 is 10.0 mL of vessel 1 diluted to 100.0 mL, and so on.
expectedObservations: The planned concentrations form a geometric series: 0.010, 0.0010, 0.00010 mol/L (values illustrative).
explanatoryNotes: Calculate first, measure second: a dilution series planned on the fly is where mistakes multiply.

steps.title: Prepare vessel 1
steps.instructions: Measure 10.0 mL of stock copper(II) sulfate solution and transfer it into vessel 1. Add distilled water until the total volume reaches 100.0 mL. Stir.
precautions: Measure the stock with the 10 mL cylinder; do not use the 100 mL cylinder for it.
expectedObservations: Vessel 1 is a clearly blue solution, visibly paler than the stock.
explanatoryNotes: The added water volume is 90.0 mL, but the concentration calculation uses the total 100.0 mL.

steps.title: Continue the series
steps.instructions: Measure 10.0 mL from vessel 1, transfer to vessel 2 and make up to 100.0 mL with distilled water. Repeat from vessel 2 to vessel 3 and from vessel 3 to vessel 4, using the freshly stirred solution each time.
precautions: Rinse the measuring cylinder with the next solution before measuring it, or use separate cylinders, to avoid cross-contamination.
expectedObservations: Each vessel is paler than the previous one; by vessel 4 the blue tint is very faint.
explanatoryNotes: Stir before every transfer; a concentration gradient inside a vessel becomes an error in the next one.

steps.title: Record the appearance of the series
steps.instructions: Arrange the vessels in order, view them against a white background in good light and record the relative colour intensity of each. Compare with the values predicted in step 1.
expectedObservations: Colour intensity decreases stepwise with calculated concentration; the trend, not exact shade matching, is the expected observation.
explanatoryNotes: Colour is a qualitative cross-check on the arithmetic, not a concentration measurement.

steps.title: Record calculations and units
steps.instructions: Record c1, V1 and V2 for every step and the resulting c2 with correct units. State the overall dilution factor from stock to vessel 4.
explanatoryNotes: The overall factor from stock to vessel 4 is 1:10^4 = 1:10000 for this plan.

troubleshooting: If two adjacent vessels look identical, re-check the transfers before concluding the calculation is wrong; incomplete rinsing is the usual cause.
If vessel 1 is as dark as the stock, the make-up volume was forgotten or too small.
If the final cylinder reading overshoots, use a dropper to correct before mixing, and record the actual volume.

measurements.label: Volume of stock taken per step
measurements.method: Measure with the 10 mL cylinder (or graduated pipette) at eye level; record the actual delivered volume.

measurements.label: Total volume per dilution step
measurements.method: Make up to 100.0 mL in the measuring cylinder or volumetric flask; record the achieved total volume.

measurements.label: Calculated concentration of each vessel
measurements.method: Computed from c1 x V1 = c2 x V2 step by step; theoretical values derived from learner measurements.

qualitativePrompts: How does the blue intensity change from vessel to vessel?
Does the step-to-step change look constant (a geometric series) or random?
Which vessel would you no longer trust to look different from pure water, and why?
errorSources: Rough volume measurements at each step multiply into large end-of-series errors.
Carrying contamination between cylinders alters the next dilution.
Comparing colours in poor light or against a coloured background biases judgment.
Reading cylinder volumes from above or below eye level causes parallax error.
interpretationGuidance: Judge the series by its trend: each vessel should be paler than the one before by a similar factor.
Treat colour as qualitative support for the calculation; concentration values come from measurements and equations, not from shade matching.
State concentrations with the significant figures the volume measurements support.

calculations.title: Concentration after one dilution step
calculations.purpose: Calculate the new concentration from the volume of stock taken and the total final volume.
assumptions: Volumes are additive at the working precision.
No solute is lost during transfer.
The stock concentration is known as stated.
calculations.unitsAndDimensions: c2 = c1 x V1 / V2; the volume units cancel (mL/mL), leaving mol/L.
calculations.significantFigureConvention: Two significant figures throughout the example because the nominal stock concentration is stated to two; round only at the end.

workedExamples.title: Worked example: first dilution step
workedExamples.result: c2 = 0.010 mol/L (1:10 dilution of the stock)
workedExamples.significantFiguresNote: 0.10 mol/L has two significant figures, so 0.010 mol/L is reported, not 0.0100.

workedExamples.title: Worked example: overall factor after four 1:10 steps
workedExamples.result: c4 = 1.0 x 10^-5 mol/L after four steps from the stock
workedExamples.significantFiguresNote: Scientific notation makes the two-significant-figure result unambiguous.

calculations.notes: Worked examples use nominal illustrative values. Learners substitute their own recorded volumes; no measured data are fabricated in this record.
